Two functions that are sometimes useful when downloading data from the internet are tempdir and tempfile. The first creates a directory with a random name that is very likely to be unique. Similarly, tempfile creates a character string (not a file) that is likely to be a unique filename. So you can run a command like this, which deletes the temporary file once the data is imported:

4. R-base Import Functions

R-base also provides import functions. These have names similar to those in the tidyverse, for example read.table, read.csv, and read.delim. However, there are a couple of important differences. To show this, we read in the data with an R-base function:

An important difference is that characters are converted to factors:

This can be avoided by setting the argument stringsAsFactors to FALSE.

This can cause confusion, because variables saved as characters in the file are converted to factors regardless of what the variable represents. In practice, it’s a good idea to make stringsAsFactors=FALSE your default approach when using the R-base parsers. After importing the data, you can easily convert the columns you want into factors.

4.1. scan

When reading in spreadsheets, many things can go wrong. The file might have a multiline header, be missing cells, or use an unexpected encoding.

A post about these common issues: The Absolute Minimum Every Software Developer Absolutely, Positively Must Know About Unicode and Character Sets (No Excuses!).

With scan, you can read in each cell of a file. For example:

The tidyverse provides read_lines, a similarly useful function.

5. Text Files versus Binary Files

Extracting data from a spreadsheet stored as a text file is probably the easiest way to bring data from a file into an R session. But spreadsheets are not always available, and the fact that you can look at a text file does not necessarily mean that extracting data from it will be simple.

6. Unicode versus ASCII

A pitfall in data science is assuming a file is an ASCII text file when, in fact, it is something else that looks a lot like an ASCII text file: a Unicode text file.

Everything on a computer ultimately needs to be converted to 0s and 1s. ASCII is an encoding that maps characters to numbers. ASCII uses 7 bits (0s and 1s), which results in $2^7 = 128$ unique items, enough to encode all the characters on an English-language keyboard. However, other languages use characters not included in this encoding. For example, the é in México is not encoded by ASCII. For this reason, a new encoding using more than 7 bits was defined: Unicode. When using Unicode, you can choose between 8, 16, and 32 bits, abbreviated UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 respectively. RStudio actually defaults to UTF-8 encoding.

A discussion on StackOverflow: R on Windows: character encoding hell.

7. Organizing Data with Spreadsheets

Things to keep in mind:

  • Be consistent - Before you start entering data, make a plan. Once you have a plan, be consistent and stick to it.
  • Choose good names for things - You want the names you pick for objects, files, and directories to be memorable, easy to spell, and descriptive. This is actually a hard balance to achieve, and it does take time and thought. One important rule to follow is do not use spaces; use underscores _ or dashes - instead. Also, avoid symbols; stick to letters and numbers.
  • Write dates as YYYY-MM-DD - To avoid confusion, use this global ISO 8601 standard.
  • No empty cells - Fill in all cells and use some common code for missing data.
  • Put just one thing in a cell - It is better to add columns to store the extra information rather than having more than one piece of information in one cell.
  • Make it a rectangle - The spreadsheet should be a rectangle.
  • Create a data dictionary - If you need to explain things, such as what the columns are or what the labels used for categorical variables are, do this in a separate file.
  • No calculations in the raw data files - Excel lets you perform calculations. Do not make this part of your spreadsheet. Code for calculations should be in a script.
  • Do not use font color or highlighting as data - Most import functions are not able to import this information. Encode this information as a variable instead.
  • Make backups - Back up your data regularly.
  • Use data validation to avoid errors - Leverage the tools in your spreadsheet software so that the process is as error-free as possible and does not cause repetitive stress injuries.
  • Save the data as text files - Save files for sharing in comma- or tab-delimited format.

entry.title: Flappy Cai Xukun: A C++ Course Project
entry.content:
About this project

This was my final project for a C++ programming course at Zhejiang University: a small side-scrolling game called Flappy Cai Xukun, written in C++ with the EasyX graphics library in Visual C++ 6.0.

The game was made because of the singer and idol Cai Xukun. In 2019 he was everywhere on the Chinese internet, and a handful of his catchphrases and moments became memes: introducing himself as a trainee who likes “singing, dancing, rap and basketball”, a dribbling clip from his NBA ambassador promo, and a line from his song Just Because You Are Too Beautiful, whose title sounds like “chicken, you’re too beautiful” in Chinese, which is why chickens show up in the game. When we had to build a game for the course, a game starring him playing basketball and rapping was the obvious choice. The code and assets are on GitHub: Bramberrr/flappycxk.

How the game works

The player character stands on a rainbow bridge in front of a scrolling starfield. Basketballs, chickens and, later, floating comments (the “danmaku” that fly across Bilibili videos) scroll in from the right, and each one has to be handled differently:

ObjectWhat to doResult
BasketballHold ↓ to get ready to catch it+5 points
Comment (appears after 100 points)Hold → to rap back at it+10 points, or −20 points and a lost life if you miss
ChickenHold ↑ to jump over itLose a life if it hits you

You start with 3 lives and get one back (up to 3) every 100 points. The other controls:

  • ← makes him stop and introduce himself, pausing the game for 6 seconds while the audio plays.
  • Shift saves a screenshot; Ctrl and Alt turn the background music off and on.
  • Esc goes back to the difficulty menu.

There are three speeds (normal, fast and very fast), set by the delay between frames: 80, 60 or 40 ms. When you run out of lives, the game shows a “you have received a lawyer’s letter” game-over screen (another meme from the time) and writes your score to record.txt.

How the code is organized

The project is small, with three source files:

  • ikun.cpp is the entry point: it starts the music and opens the menu.
  • cxk.cpp has the game itself: the menus, the main loop, drawing, input, collisions and the starfield.
  • media.cpp plays the music and sound clips with the Windows mciSendString API, and saves screenshots.

The menus are images with clickable regions, read from EasyX mouse messages. The game loop runs at a fixed delay and does the same steps every frame:

The objects on screen are kept in a linked list. New ones are added at the tail, with a 1-in-5 chance each frame, but only if the previous one is far enough away; objects that scroll off the left edge are removed:

A few small touches I was proud of at the time: the character is animated from a six-frame dribbling sequence, basketballs bob up and down randomly as they fly in, the rainbow bridge is drawn line by line by stepping the hue, and each star scrolls at its own speed, with faster stars drawn brighter for a sense of depth:

Looking back

It’s a very “first big C++ project” codebase: everything lives in global state and one big loop, input is polled with GetAsyncKeyState, objects are managed with malloc/free by hand, and the audio clips can pause the whole game. But it was a fun way to learn how a game loop, sprite animation, collision checks and a linked list fit together, and it definitely made the course demo memorable.

entry.title: The "3D Printer Car": Our SUPCON Cup Robot
entry.content:
About this project

This is the robot my team built for the 14th SUPCON Cup Robot Competition at Zhejiang University, in spring 2019. It was my second time in the competition. I led a team with two teammates, and we entered under the name “Bamboo Rats: 3 Yuan Each, 3 for 10”, a meme that was popular at the time.

The robot drives around a field of grid lines, stops at the intersections, and picks up objects with a gripper. This note is adapted from our technical report.

The idea: a 3D printer on wheels

From earlier experience, I expected that a gripper mounted on a robot arm would wobble, especially when the motor current isn’t steady. A 3D printer, on the other hand, positions its nozzle very precisely along X, Y and Z rails. So instead of an arm, we built a small 3D-printer-style gantry on top of a car. The gripper moves along straight axes, which keeps it steady while lining up and after it has picked something up.

Mechanical design

Chassis. Four DC gear motors with wheels and couplings drive the robot. The chassis is two layers of acrylic connected by copper standoffs. The space between the layers holds the battery, the low-level controller, the motor drivers, a breadboard and the switches.

Upper body. The upper body is a wooden box that works like a 3D printer, with four motions:

  • Up and down (Z): a stepper motor turns a lead screw, and the nut raises or lowers the whole upper body. Guide rods and aluminum angle keep it aligned.
  • Forward and back (X): a stepper motor drives a timing belt over pulleys, moving a slider along guide rods to extend or retract the gripper.
  • Left and right (Y): the same belt-and-slider setup on the other axis, for fine sideways adjustment.
  • Gripper: a digital servo opens and closes an iron claw. The jaws are padded with heat-resistant sponge for grip.

The belts are fixed to the sliders with small 3D-printed clamps:

The plates were laser-cut from 2D drawings:

PartMaterial
Chassis platesAcrylic
Upper bodyWood
Shafts and guide rodsSteel and aluminum
GripperIron
Gripper paddingHeat-resistant sponge

Motor selection

We used JGA25-370 gear motors: 12 V, 10 kg·cm of torque, with 6.5 cm wheels. By our calculation, four of them can move at least 10 kg, far more than the robot weighs.

Sensors

The robot has 8 infrared line sensors: 4 at the front and 4 in the middle. The front row follows the line and counts the grid lines it crosses. The middle row tells the robot exactly when it is centered on an intersection, so it can stop there and turn accurately.

Each sensor board is a 4-channel infrared module. Each channel has its own IR emitter and receiver, and an LM339 comparator with hysteresis turns the analog signal into a clean on/off output without flickering at the threshold. The modules run on 4–6 V and draw 30–40 mA with all four channels on.

Electronics

  • Low-level controller: ATmega128. An 8-bit AVR microcontroller (up to 16 MIPS at 16 MHz, 128 KB flash, 4 KB EEPROM, 4 KB SRAM). We chose it mainly because it has enough I/O pins for all the motors and sensors.
  • High-level controller: Raspberry Pi with a camera, for image recognition. It sends commands to the ATmega128.

What made it different

  1. A gantry instead of an arm. The 3D-printer-style structure moves the gripper along straight axes, so the robot stays steady and doesn’t shake.
  2. Two rows of line sensors. Separate rows for following and for stopping made the turns at intersections much more precise.

What was hard

  1. Line following sometimes lost the line, and counting grid lines wasn’t always reliable: the robot could overshoot and miss a line.
  2. Communication delay between the Raspberry Pi and the ATmega128.
  3. Power: with four DC motors, three steppers and a servo, the battery struggled to supply enough current.
